Name: Adam
Transcript: Good to see you again. Last time was March, before the season started. So, to begin, what's the plot like for you now, at midsummer?

Name: Nell
Transcript: It's a jungle. I said it would be, and it is. I am very good at predicting myself. I have been maybe four times since May. Four. The calendar in the kitchen with two mornings a week, it's still there, I look at it, it looks at me. And every time I go to the plot I see only what I have not done. The weeds up to my knees, the path you cannot see any more, the beans I didn't plant. I stand at the gate and I see it all at once. And I come home feeling worse than before I went. Is crazy. I go there to feel better and I come home worse.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Can you take me through a visit, the last time you went?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Sunday. I parked, I got Daria out of the car seat, she wanted to walk, so it took ten minutes from the car park. Matei ran ahead to his sunflowers. And I came to the gate and I saw it. The jungle. And my stomach went down. Every time, the same. Then I just start. I don't plan, I just pull, pull, pull, the weeds by the path, fast, like I'm racing somebody. One hour. I look at my phone every ten minutes because I have to make lunch. And Daria is eating something, and Matei is shouting mama look, mama look, and I say yes, beautiful, without looking. And then we go home and I can see where I pulled, a little square, and all the rest still jungle.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Feeling worse than before you went. What's that like?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Like walking into a room where everybody knows you did something wrong. You know this feeling? Nobody says anything, but everybody knows. I walk up the path and the other plots are perfect, the old men with their straight lines, and then mine. Mine is like the house of somebody who died. And I feel them looking. Maybe they don't look. Maybe they don't care at all. But I feel it on my back, like a hand.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Like everybody knows.

Name: Nell
Transcript: And then they did know. In June the committee sent me a letter. Official, with a logo. Your plot is not being cultivated to the required standard. Please contact the secretary within fourteen days. I read it in the car, outside the nursery, and I cried. Proper crying, with Daria in the back asking mama why are you crying, mama is it the radio. A letter. Like from the council, like I am in trouble. Like somebody walked past my plot with a clipboard and wrote my name down. And this is exactly what happened. Somebody walked past and wrote my name down.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What was it like, being written down?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Shame. Big shame. I am not a person who gets letters like this. I always pay first, I always fill the forms correct, I always do everything they ask. Eleven years in this country and I never get one letter like this. And now for vegetables. Chris said, it's only a letter, just give it back, give back the plot, who cares. But I don't give things back. I'm not a person who gives things back. If I give back every hard thing, I would be in the village still. So I phoned the secretary and I said, I'm sorry, I have small children, I will do better. Like a schoolgirl.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Since the letter, what's it like walking up the path?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Worse. Now I know they know. Before I thought maybe. Now I know somebody wrote my name. So I go early, very early, half past six, when nobody is there. Or I go on a Thursday evening when the old men are at home for their dinner. I park at the far side, by the fence, not by the gate. I'm hiding, I know this. I'm a grown woman hiding from pensioners with clipboards. But I can't help it. When I see somebody coming I bend down and pretend I'm doing something very important with the onions.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And the children, in all this?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Oh, the children love it. They love it more than me now. Matei has his own patch, I gave him a corner by the shed, and he planted sunflowers. And they are taller than him now. Every Sunday he stands next to them and I take a photo, and he says mama, measure me, and we measure, and the sunflowers are winning. He has a book about sunflowers from the library. He told his teacher how a sunflower turns its head to the sun in the morning. He explained it to the whole class. That part is exactly what I wanted. Exactly. When I see him standing there with his sunflowers, it's, yes. That's it. That's what I wanted.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What's that like, seeing him with them?

Name: Nell
Transcript: I want to cry also, but a different crying. Happy. Proud. He knows where food comes from now. Well, he knows where sunflowers come from, is a start. And Daria, she has a little watering can, pink, and she waters everything. The sunflowers, the weeds, the path, my shoes. Especially my shoes. They are happy there. They don't see the jungle. For them it's not a jungle, it's a forest, it's an adventure. They don't see what I see.

Name: Adam
Transcript: They don't see what you see. What's that like for you?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Good, and a bit lonely. Good because I want them to have this, the adventure, the not seeing. Children should not see the jungle. They should see a forest. But lonely because I am the only one who sees it. Chris doesn't come, he's working. The children don't see it. So it's me, alone, seeing the jungle, with two happy children in it. Like a mother at a party who sees the mess and everybody else is dancing. This is being a mother, I think, a lot of the time. Seeing the mess so they don't have to.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And the time for yourself, the one thing that's yours?

Name: Nell
Transcript: There is none. The deckchair is still in the shed. Folded. I bought it in April, nice one, striped, and it has never been open. Not one time. When I do get a minute down there, alone, maybe an hour while Chris has the kids, I spend it weeding. Weeding and weeding and feeling guilty about all the weeding I didn't do. Even the guilt is not mine. Even the guilt is for the plot. I wanted one thing that is mine and now I have one more thing that I'm failing at.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Have you thought about giving it up?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Every week. Every single week. Sunday night I think, that's it, I write to the secretary. And then Monday morning Matei asks me, mama, when are we going to the plot? Are the sunflowers bigger? And I cannot say to him we're not going any more. I cannot do this. So I suppose it's his now, really. The plot is his and I am the help. I carry the watering cans, I drive the car, I do the weeding. He is the farmer. I am the help.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You're the help. What's that like?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Funny, a bit. And a bit sad. Funny because he's five and he gives me orders. Mama, water there. Mama, not that one, that's a sunflower. He's a very strict farmer. I don't know where he gets it. And sad because I wanted one thing that was mine and I gave it to him without deciding. I didn't decide. It just happened, one Sunday, I was carrying his watering can and I thought, oh. This is his. But when I see his face, it's okay. It's okay to be the help, for this face.

Name: Adam
Transcript: In March you talked about your buni's garden. Is that still with you?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Yes, and this is the strange part. My mother came. In June, for three weeks, to help with the children because the nursery was closed. And while I was at work, she went to the plot. Every day. With Daria in the pushchair. And in three weeks she cleared half of it. Half. She dug it, she planted beans, courgettes, dill, peppers, everything in lines, like a soldier. In three weeks she did what I didn't do in three months. And she didn't laugh at me this time. She didn't say anything. She just worked.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What was that like for you?

Name: Nell
Transcript: I came after work, the first time I saw it, and it looked like my buni's garden. The lines, the dill, the beans on sticks the way they do it at home, not the way they do it here. And for one minute I was so happy. Like I opened a door and the village was there. And then the next minute I felt like a visitor. Like it was her garden and I was the girl again, the girl who carries the bucket and spills it on her legs. I was standing on my own plot like a guest.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Like a guest on your own plot.

Name: Nell
Transcript: And how can I be angry? She saved my plot. She saved me from the committee. The secretary walked past and he said, well done, Nell, what a difference. To me! He said it to me. And it was her. And I said thank you, thank you. And I said thank you mama, thank you so much, and I meant it. But inside I was, I don't have the word in English. In Romanian also I don't have it. Small. Grateful and small at the same time. Like when you are a teenager and your mother fixes your homework, and it's better, and you hate it.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And how was it, with your mother, while she was here?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Good. Mostly good. We were close, the three weeks. In the evening, when the children were asleep, she told me things about buni's garden that I didn't know. That buni planted the beans the day after the first thunder, every year, that was her rule. That she talked to the peppers. I never knew she talked to the peppers. My mother laughed telling me, but she was a bit sad also, because the garden is gone now. And I thought, my mother had buni's garden for her whole childhood, the same as me in the summers. And she left it. She chose to leave it. And now she comes to England and makes it again on my plot, in three weeks, like she never left.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What's it like now she's gone home?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Now I have two plots. Hers and mine. Her half is beautiful, everything growing, people stop and look. My half is still jungle. Is very funny if you think about it. Two halves, two women. Hers is good. But the dill, I cook with her dill now, I put it in the soup, and the whole kitchen smells like home. Like my buni's kitchen. So I am grateful. I am. Even when I'm small, I'm grateful.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And your body, with all this?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Tired. Just tired. I did my back in, a little bit, carrying Daria on one side and a watering can on the other, up the hill from the car park. My body says no and I go anyway. That's me, that's how I always am. In March I told you there is a good tired. I remember I said this. Now there is no good tired. Is just tired. The grey one. The plot became one more grey thing.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Just tired. What's that like?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Like I am behind, all the time, with everything. Behind at work, behind with the washing, behind with the plot, behind with phoning my buni. Behind is my whole body. I wake up already behind. And the plot was supposed to be the one place where I'm not behind, where I'm just there. And instead it's the place where I'm most behind of all, where you can see how behind I am, with your eyes, in weeds.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Is there anything else, about the plot now, that I haven't asked?

Name: Nell
Transcript: Can I say something? I think in March I was a bit, dreaming. The deckchair, the book, the summer like my buni. I was dreaming. Now I'm awake. Is not bad, to be awake. Is just awake. I see what it is now. It's a lot of work, and it's the children's, and it's my mother's half, and it's a letter from the committee. That's what it is. Not a dream. I don't know yet if I like what it is. But at least I see it.
